title: Vikings to Rotate Players Under Brian Flores to Combat Mexico City Altitude Challenges, NBC Sports Reports
body:
The Minnesota Vikings have unveiled a tactical rotation plan to counter the thin air of Mexico City, while the San Francisco 49ers have opted for a more conventional approach—spending a full week at altitude in Colorado to acclimate before their Week 11 showdown at Estadio Azteca. The divergent strategies highlight how NFL teams are adapting to the unique challenges posed by the league’s first regular‑season game at a high‑elevation venue since the 2016 International Series in Mexico City.

The 49ers, who will travel to Mexico City after a brief stint at the Denver Broncos’ training facilities, are banking on physiological adaptation. By training at roughly 5,280 feet above sea level, the team hopes to mitigate the reduced oxygen levels that can sap stamina and impair decision‑making. Head coach Kyle Shanahan has reportedly incorporated a mix of cardio drills, breathing exercises, and a modified practice schedule to simulate the slower recovery times players will experience on game day. “We want our guys to feel as normal as possible when they step onto the field,” Shanahan told reporters, emphasizing that the extra week is a proactive measure rather than a reaction to any specific deficiency.

In contrast, Vikings head coach Brian Flores has taken a logistical route, planning to rotate his roster throughout the game to keep players fresh in the thin air. Flores, who has a reputation for creative personnel management, said the Vikings will employ a “mini‑four‑quarter” system, substituting key skill‑position players after the first quarter and re‑injecting them later in the second half. The plan also includes a deeper reliance on the special teams unit, which traditionally endures less sustained physical exertion than offensive and defensive squads. “We can’t control the environment, but we can control the snap count and the fatigue factor,” Flores explained during the pre‑game press conference.

Analysts note that both approaches have precedent in NFL history, though neither has been tested extensively at an altitude exceeding 2,200 meters, the elevation of Mexico City. The last major test came in 2016 when the Dallas Cowboys and Los Angeles Rams faced each other in the city; the Cowboys, who arrived a day early, appeared less winded in the fourth quarter, while the Rams relied heavily on a rotating backfield to sustain momentum. Recent sports‑science research suggests that a week of high‑altitude exposure can improve red‑blood‑cell count and aerobic capacity, but the benefits plateau after 48‑72 hours, raising questions about the marginal gains the 49ers hope to secure.

The Vikings’ rotation scheme could also influence the broader strategic landscape of the league. If Flores’ plan proves effective, other teams may adopt similar “fresh‑leg” tactics for future high‑altitude or extreme‑weather matchups, potentially reshaping roster construction and in‑game decision‑making. However, the strategy carries risks: frequent substitutions can disrupt offensive rhythm and defensive cohesion, and the limited bench depth of some teams may expose them to injury or fatigue elsewhere in the season.

As the two franchises prepare for a contest that pits a methodical acclimation program against a dynamic rotation system, the outcome will offer valuable data on how best to contend with altitude in the modern NFL. Regardless of which approach prevails, the game will serve as a litmus test for coaches seeking to blend science, strategy, and player welfare in increasingly diverse playing conditions. The result could set a new standard for preparation ahead of the league’s expanding international schedule, where altitude, heat, and time‑zone shifts are becoming routine hurdles for teams chasing a Super Bowl berth.
